stories.headline: Air India may hire departed Garuda CFO
stories.title: Air India may hire departed Garuda CFO
stories.summary: Air India Ltd. is considering appointing Balagopal Kunduvara as chief financial officer, tapping the veteran of Singapore Airlines Ltd. to help revive the Indian carrier’s finances after a record loss, according to people familiar with the matter.Kunduvara is a frontrunner for the position, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private deliberations. Most recently, he was finance chief for Garuda Indonesia, a position he recently left after holding the job for little more than a year.Also read | Australia's Qantas Airways to cut 850 jobs as AI takes off, back-office work shifts to IndiaPrior to that, Kunduvara spent more than two decades at Singapore Airlines, which is a partial owner of Air India alongside conglomerate Tata Group. Air India is seeking 100 billion rupees ($1.1 billion) in funding from its owners, Bloomberg News reported previously.An Air India spokesman didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.Air India is in the midst of a turnaround effort led by newly appointed Chief Executive Officer Tewolde Gebremariam after it posted a loss of more than 220 billion rupees last fiscal year. Tewolde has said he will focus on cutting costs.Kunduvara announced his departure from Garuda in a post on LinkedIn. While his time at the airline had been “relatively brief,” it coincided with an important period in the company’s transformation, he said.A spokesperson for Garuda confirmed that Kunduvara had left the company.Kunduvara would take the CFO role as Air India faces high fuel costs due to the war in Iran. It also has to contend with geopolitical challenges that include a drop in traffic to the Middle East and being barred from Pakistani airspace, which forces west-bound flights from its main hub in New Delhi to take a circuitous route.Also read | Airlines go premium as demand for business-class seats outpaces economyTewolde, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines Group, has been looking to bolster Air India’s underperforming cargo business, and integrate key departments at Air India and its low-cost arm, Air India Express, to cut costs.The CEO is also looking at whether more flights to Europe and the US should be routed through Mumbai instead of Delhi to get around the Pakistani airspace closing.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

body: to help revive the Indian carrier’s finances after a record loss, according to people familiar with the matter.
Kunduvara is a frontrunner for the position, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private deliberations.
Most recently, he was finance chief for Garuda Indonesia, a position he recently left after holding the job for little more than a year.

Also read | Australia's Qantas Airways to cut 850 jobs as AI takes off, back-office work shifts to IndiaPrior to that, Kunduvara spent more than two decades at Singapore Airlines, which is a partial owner of Air India alongside conglomerate Tata Group.
Air India is seeking 100 billion rupees ($1.1 billion) in funding from its owners, Bloomberg News reported previously.
An Air India spokesman didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tewolde has said he will focus on cutting costs.
Kunduvara announced his departure from Garuda in a post on Linked.
While his time at the airline had been “relatively brief,” it coincided with an important period in the company’s transformation, he said.
A spokesperson for Garuda confirmed that Kunduvara had left the company.
Kunduvara would take the CFO role as Air India faces high fuel costs due to the war in Iran.

It also has to contend with geopolitical challenges that include a drop in traffic to the Middle East and being barred from Pakistani airspace, which forces west-bound flights from its main hub in New Delhi to take a circuitous route.

Also read | Airlines go premium as demand for business-class seats outpaces economyTewolde, who previously led Ethiopian Airlines Group, has been looking to bolster Air India’s underperforming cargo business, and integrate key departments at Air India and its low-cost arm, Air India Express, to cut costs.
The CEO is also looking at whether more flights to Europe and the US should be routed through Mumbai instead of Delhi to get around the Pakistani airspace closing.

stories.headline: Supreme Court seeks action plan on Delhi-NCR vehicular pollution in 2 weeks
stories.title: Supreme Court seeks action plan on Delhi-NCR vehicular pollution in 2 weeks
stories.summary: Supreme Court seeks action plan on Delhi-NCR vehicular pollution in 2 weeks
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
event term: 'supreme court' in summary weight 26.4
article_sentences: A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana directed the governments to submit plans covering vehicular movement, emission standards and measures to curb polluting vehicles.
The Supreme Court has sought a detailed action plan within two weeks from Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan to tackle vehicular pollution in the National Capital Region (NCR).

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana directed the Delhi government, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), Delhi Police’s traffic department and the three state governments to submit plans covering vehicular movement, emission standards and measures to curb polluting vehicles.
The court sought details of the criteria and procedures used to ensure compliance with vehicle emission standards.
It also asked how strictly the rules governing Pollution Under Control (PUC) certificates were being enforced.
The bench sought details of action taken against old vehicles and those failing to meet prescribed standards, including the number of vehicles checked and challans issued.
The vehicular pollution matter will next be heard on November 23.
The court’s directions come amid worsening air quality in Delhi-NCR.
The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) invoked Stage III of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) on Friday, ahead of Diwali.
The revised Stage III framework comprises a 10-point action plan for the NCR, which includes Delhi and parts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan.
One of the major measures is a ban on several dust-generating construction and demolition activities.
These include excavation, piling, demolition, brickwork, road construction, major welding operations, painting, polishing and the movement of construction materials on unpaved roads.

stories.headline: Five Days Left to Comment on China's Solar Technology Export Curbs, and India Is Already Affected
stories.title: Five Days Left to Comment on China's Solar Technology Export Curbs, and India Is Already Affected
stories.summary: China's Ministry of Commerce has proposed adding 12 photovoltaic manufacturing technologies to its export-control list, with public consultation closing on 15 November. The draft is part of a wider revision of the technology catalogue that also covers artificial intelligence and biotechnology. Beijing cites national security, arguing that solar technologies are increasingly used in sensitive areas such as aerospace and defence. What would be banned, and what restricted The outright ban would cover processes used to make thin silicon wafers, perovskite and tandem solar cells, and large-scale fluidised-bed polysilicon production. Reporting on the draft's thresholds says the tandem ban applies to cells on wafers of at least 182 mm with efficiency of 30% or more, and to large-area modules of at least one square metre. Fluidised-bed polysilicon is cheaper and more energy-efficient than the dominant Siemens process. TOPCon, HJT and XBC cell manufacturing technologies would be restricted rather than prohibited, meaning licensing rather than a flat ban. The draft does not stop finished panels, cells or wafers from being exported. Exporters must already register certain overseas technology transfers, a requirement that took effect on 16 October and applies until the catalogue is formally revised. China already curbed exports of solar-manufacturing technology to India, besides battery cells. India's exposure The draft extends controls to technology transfers worldwide. India's installed solar capacity reached 171.05 GW at the end of September, including 20.79 GW added in the first half of FY27. Module manufacturing capacity has passed 200 GW. Upstream, the picture is thinner. Union Minister Pralhad Joshi put cell capacity at about 45 GW at the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, while industry voices there said effective capacity is below 40 GW, with ingot and wafer capacity under 1% of the total and commercial-scale polysilicon production yet to begin. That is exactly the layer the draft targets. The Indian Solar Manufacturers Association ( ISMA ) is now prioritising ingots, wafers and polysilicon, per coverage of the summit. Thin-wafer processes and fluidised-bed polysilicon are two of the banned items, so Indian plans in those segments would have to rely on non-Chinese technology. The European route India's response is already visible. At the same summit, IB Solar signed an MoU with German technology partners to set up what is described as India's first Centre of Excellence for solar technology in Uttar Pradesh, backed by the National Solar Energy Federation of India. Separately, the company signed an MoU with three German firms to develop a 2 GW TOPCon cell line at its Indian facility, as reported by us last week. TOPCon underpins several of India's recent cell plants. In September that Premier Energies commissioned a 7 GW TOPCon cell plant, taking its cell capacity to 10.6 GW, and that Alpex Solar inaugurated a 2.2 GW TOPCon facility in Mathura. Those plants are built. Others like Saatvik Green energy are testing production at a 4 GW cell plant in Odisha. Vikram Solar is also hoping to start a massive 10 GW facility by December. The open question is whether future expansions, upgrades and equipment support would face licensing delays if the restrictions are finalised as drafted. What to watch The consultation closes on 15 November, after which China's regulators will decide whether to keep the thresholds. Three points matter for Indian manufacturers: whether TOPCon stays on the restricted rather than banned list, how the registration regime is applied in practice, and whether Indian developers can substitute European or domestic equipment fast enough to protect expansion schedules. For India, the case for building a technology base, rather than only assembly lines, has become a supply-security argument as much as an industrial one.
